summary: A short query asking whether any ARPANET host offered an interpreter for MIX, Knuth's hypothetical computer, and an assembler for its language MIXAL, for students of The Art of Computer Programming. If not, the author asked that some host provide one. RFC 494 and RFC 485 follow on.

eli5.summary: Someone asked if any network computer could run the pretend computer from a famous programming book, so students could try the examples.

subtitle: A one-paragraph query asking whether any ARPANET host offers an interpreter and assembler for Knuth's MIX computer.

tldr.problem: Students of Knuth's Art of Computer Programming needed a way to run programs for MIX, the book's hypothetical computer, and to assemble programs written in MIXAL.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC simply asks whether any ARPA Network host already offers a MIX interpreter and a MIXAL assembler, and if not, asks whether some host will make them available cheaply.
tldr.outcome: It is a request, not a specification. The RFC itself records no answer.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 473 as Unknown, and it is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It is a historical query rather than a specification.

sections.title: The Question
sections.content: This RFC, from D. Walden of BBN-NET and dated 28 February 1973, is a single question. It asks whether an interpreter for MIX, Knuth's hypothetical computer, is available on any ARPA Network host, together with an assembler for the MIX assembly language, MIXAL.
sections.eli5: MIX is a pretend computer from a book. The author asks whether anyone on the network has a program that can act like it.

sections.title: Who Wants It and Why
sections.content:
The author describes the audience as students of the Art of Computer Programming. Having MIX and MIXAL available on a network host would, in the RFC's words, be a considerable service to all of them.

The RFC adds that, if no host has these tools, it hopes some Network Host will make them available cheaply.
sections.eli5: People reading the book want to try its examples on a real machine, and a pretend computer needs a helper program to run on a real one.

sections.title: What the RFC Settles
sections.content: The RFC defines no protocol and no format, and it gives no answer to its own question. It is an early example of the RFC series being used to ask the community for a resource rather than to specify a standard.
sections.eli5: It is a note on a bulletin board that says, does anyone have this? The note does not say who answered.
